Ridden: Macfox's X1S Commuter E-Bike Surprises With Sturdy and Customizable Build at $1,400
46 photos
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution
One of the benefits of writing for autoevolution is that I often have the pleasure of testing all sorts of vehicles. One of the industries I often research is e-biking, and this time around we’ll be diving into an e-bikes dubbed the X1S from Macfox, a brand that I'm not testing for the second time, and if I may, I continue to be pleasantly surprised.
Folks, the name Macfox is one that we’ve shed light upon before, when we tested their oversized X7L e-bike earlier this year. They have, however, shown signs of life as early as 2022, and since then, have slowly crept into home after home with their solid and accessible rides.
Pleased with the free press review that we completed on the X7L , Macfox asked me to give one of their entry-level models a go, in particular, the X1S, a bike that bears a similar frame to the X7L, but a bit smaller. However, as I would soon find out, smaller does not mean any less capable, and the X1S actually surprised me in several ways.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution Before going on, however, allow me to point out that I had the occasion to test the European version as I'm currently stationed out here, awaiting to attend EICMA in Milan. So the specs and what we learned about the X1S will differ a bit from what US-destined versions can achieve.
Design Evaluation As one of the smaller e-bikes from Macfox, the X1S distinguishes itself from the X7L with a smaller frame and wheels that are tighter too. Instead of 5-inch rubbers that the X7L exhibited, the X1S has 4-inch tires, and a tread that’s more inclined for tarmac instead of dirt roads and trails. That, however, doesn’t mean it won’t feel at home on a dirt road, it does, put you’ll need to be a bit wearier of punctures.
The frame on the other hand, is still one that resembles the whole scrambler style of rides, and oddly enough, in a good way. It actually feels a bit motorcycle-like on the turns due to its trail and head tube angle; we’ll talk more about that shortly.
The seat is also an elongated one, and since there is a set of foot pegs on this one, just like on the X7L, two riders can enjoy a trip. Macfox mentions a peak rider weight of 100 kg (220 lbs), but I did try and push this limit with a friend and I, and even at 125 kg (276 lbs), the X1S still moved, albeit a bit sluggishly.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution The frame also never ceases to amaze me in terms of build quality. From the first few minutes on the X1S, I remarked just how sturdy the backbone is. It just feels solid, and there’s no doubt about it. It’s steel, so it does weigh a bit; Macfox mentions a weight of 30 kg (66 lbs) for this thing.
One other aspect of this sort of frame that you do need to consider, especially if you’re a taller rider, is the inability to modify seat height. As a result, pedaling on this style of e-bike can be a bit uncomfortable, and often, they are equipped with throttle so you can just sit back and enjoy the ride. The X1S does have throttle functionality, and it does play a crucial role in our ability to do wheelies with this one.
However, I had a bit of a different experience with the throttle function because in Europe, Macfox limits its use to just 6 kph (3.7 mph) and is very strict on sharing the information needed to unlock the full capability of the bike. Most likely, there are folks in your town that know how to unlock these babies, or you can find instructions online.
For the sake of the review, I didn’t tamper with this aspect of the bike, as that’s how Macfox sells it in the EU, and frankly, I don’t mind much. It does make it a bit difficult to stay in the saddle for more than 20 km (12 mph) at a time before you need to stretch those legs.
For Europe, the X1S is also limited to a peak of a nice and legal 25 kph, but for the US, it’s limited to 20 mph (32 kph), so plenty of speed to get around town, and in NA, throttle use is unrestricted, so enjoy.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution Another important change that applies to European models is the motor strength. Nominally, it runs at 250 W, whereas, US models include a 500 W motor, both are strapped to the rear hub and both versions are said to peak at 750 W.
What I was unable to find for European versions is torque output, but what I can say is that the X1S had no trouble tackling 15-degree hills in my area, even with the single-speed drivetrain setup, another reason why throttle use would be fantastic on this version and why we can really sit in the saddle for too long.
For riders in the US, the X1S does boast a peak of 65 Nm (48 lb-ft) of torque.
This brings us to range, a wildly controversial side of any e-bike ride, mainly because of the countless different aspects that affect each ride. Yet, for the X1S, we’re told that a peak of 50 km (31 miles) is the max range here, yet my experience was a wildly different one, and in the best way possible; I also know why I pulled the number I did.
In terms of suspension, the X1S is only sporting a front fork with a reported 120 mm of travel, ample room for bump-absorbing action, which is essential considering that it’s not an adjustable fork, at least, not the version I was riding. Other X1S models do appear to have adjustability, so it depends on the model year, who you get it from, and if any modifications have been made.
Speaking of which, Macfox designs the bike as a whole to be highly customizable, and with countless accessories online and even on their website, we can create more than just an X1S, you can make your OWN X1S, as unique as you.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution The last traits of the design that I need to mention include the headlight at the front, the trigger for the rear light – it even has turn signals but no actual lights – and the most important, disc brakes with hydraulic pistons and calipers that seem a bit overkill for the discs but help stop on a gosh darned dime if needed. Toss on a couple of fenders, and you’re off.
Ride Time In terms of the riding experience, things were actually rather surprising. I had ridden scrambler/bobber-style e-bikes before, and this is one of the ones that I found rather decent in terms of comfort. While the frame style does force your legs to never fully extend, if we shuffle back on the seat a bit, we can access a bit more legroom.
Since the throttle doesn’t help out on European versions, keep in mind that the specs I'll be pointing out are based solely on pedal assist.
Since legroom has a whole lot to do with comfort , I'll continue there before heading into more important territory. The front suspension on the X1S is, as you’d expect from 120 mm of travel, it is squishy, but the rear could use some shocks, especially if you hit some larger cracks, come off a curb, or anything or the sort. But, to reduce vibrations from the tarmac and even handle hardpack dirt roads with small gravel, it’s fine.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution You can tamper with tire pressure to play around with some softness, at the cost of range, that is. The tires do play a pivotal role in softening up the road on such a burly frame.
One aspect of riding this e-bike that I found rather interesting is the way it takes turns. Much like a motorcycle, or at least, the one’s I've ridden, once you commit to a corner, the bike takes over and does the work for you, which makes it rather easy to turn, but you do need to be making a conscious decision to turn as it’ll pull you in the direction you’re going. I like it.
In terms of how much abuse and vibrations the whole system can take, here too i was pleased, with the frame really feeling solid on any terrain I tested. Nothing bangs around and makes wild noises either, except the occasional brake pad touching the disc where torsional forces may be too much for the spoke layup. It is a steel frame, so it will bend a bit but can take quite the abuse.
Lately, there has been a renewed interest in steel tubing for bikes, and countless brands are now crafting nothing but steel bikes, be they custom or mass-produced. It’s inexpensive and easy to work with, but a dash heavy, as we all know.
Onto the more important aspects such as power and range. First off, I mentioned that a 250 W motor is in place here, and since I was only riding with pedal assist, it’s difficult for me to tell you a precise acceleration time. However, in third speed, the one that allows us to access all the power from this motor, I was reaching 25 kph in around 10-12 seconds or so. I do weight around 77 kg (170 lbs) and sometimes, I was off to a rough start.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution What I can mention is that if the throttle was working, that time could be reduced drastically, and would make it easier to enjoy a ride with a friend on the rear, if you don’t overload the bike too much.
Yet, throttle function would also greatly influence how much range we can squeeze out of the 13 Ah battery (48 V ecosystem). Keep in mind that Macfox mentions a peak of just 50 km for the European version, but somehow, I was experiencing a whole lot more, and as mentioned, I know why: the lack of throttle.
As such, I was always in pedal assist mode, and usually, in the second of the three speed settings, staying at around 20 kph on average. This, somehow, granted access to an average of over 50 km, 55-60 km (up to 37 miles), but that is on a full charge. If I stayed at 10-15% before recharging, yes, 50 km is a clearly on the menu.
Keep in mind that the X1S can be equipped with another battery as well, allowing us to double our riding time and possibly use it for delivery services.
Recharging such a big battery does, usually take a while, and in the X1S’ case, up to six hours is what you’ll have to wait for before riding out again. But, if you recharge your battery after riding, you’ll never have to experience that sort of downtime.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution This battery is a removable one, which does help if you live on the upper levels of an apartment building; elevators need to be big to fit this inside too, and you can do so in a vertical position with some light acrobatics.
Since the drivetrain is one aspect that I had mixed feelings about, I want to take a moment and mention the importance of having some gearing available. A single-speed setup is not optimum for tackling hills, and while I could make it up any in my town, on some of them, you can hear the motor struggle a bit. Speaking of struggle, I was surprised at how much quieter the X1S motor is in comparison to the X7L. Sometimes, the treads on the tarmac make more noise.
What I noticed about the X1S is that it’s rocking a cadence sensor, as it’s the only one that behaves in the way that the bike displays, and if you’ve ever ridden with one of these, you know you can trick the motor into thinking you’re asking for power, even though you’re pedaling just to keep the rotation of the cranks going, without actually placing any pressure on the pedals themselves.
Considering the single-speed setup, after 20 kph or so, your pedaling doesn’t do much anymore except keep the motor engaged.
As for braking, at 25 kph (15.5 mph) an hour of max speed, these brakes are just downright mean, and it is a feature that I greatly appreciated about the bike. Sure, the treads and massive contact patch help in the mix, but I was seeing braking distances of around 4 m (12 ft) with this one, so if you ride by looking ahead, you’ll have time to stop. Discs with 180 mm diameter are found on this one.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution For night riding, the solid headlight does one heck of a job to light up your way, so no issues there, and at the rear, the taillight is definitely wide enough to be seen but doesn’t flash or shine brighter as you press the brakes.
Conclusion Now, the X1S isn’t perfect, in the sense that it’s not a bicycle designed for every rider out there, and if you have knee issues, you’ll clearly want to beg Macfox to unlock that throttle if you’re in Europe.
The throttle function is also an essential key to the puzzle for e-bikes of this style, and to see this brand really hold onto their law-abiding distribution can be considered a benefit and a drawback, depending on if you’re the rider or seller.
But, a solid frame, good components that can take a thrashing, and a price tag of $1,400 for US riders makes this one a decent option to go for, especially if you want an e-bike that can also be customized to express the color of your own soul.
Not bad there, Macfox, not bad at all.
Pros :
Sturdy Frame
Customizable
Strong Components
Good Range
Cons :
No Throttle (EU Version)
A Bit Heavy
Single speed
Rating : 4.0 / 5.0
